Christine Lagarde
The President of the European Central Bank 
SPEECH
Acting in time
Keynote speech by Christine Lagarde, President of the ECB, at the 36th Frankfurt European Banking Congress
Frankfurt am Main, 20 November 2026
It is a pleasure to be back at this congress. This is the eighth time I have spoken here as President of the ECB, and it will sadly be the last.
In preparing for today, I reread those speeches. The topics have varied, from growth and inflation to capital markets and the Single Market.
But one concern runs through all of them: how to make Europe stronger, so that its prosperity is driven by its own strengths and less exposed to decisions taken elsewhere.
For many years, the challenges we discussed here were old ones. We had fallen short of our ambitions for the Single Market. Our growth relied too heavily on external demand for an economy of our size, and our competitiveness was slowly eroding.
Those challenges have not gone away. But in recent years, new ones have been layered on top. Dependencies that we once saw as a normal part of an open economy, from critical raw materials to technology, can now be used against us. That has made economic sovereignty a challenge in its own right.
The old challenges and the new ones have something in common.
Five centuries ago, Machiavelli compared the problems of states to a fever that, at the start, is “easy to cure but difficult to detect” and, in time, becomes “easy to detect but difficult to cure”.
Both kinds of challenge are of this sort. By the time everyone can see the need to act, the best time to act has usually passed.
Acting early, before the case is obvious, is one of the hardest things a policymaker has to do. It means paying a price up front for a distant pay-off. And if nothing goes wrong, those who acted can easily appear to have paid that price for nothing.
Today I would like to reflect on how Europe can still act early, drawing on how we have approached this at the ECB and on what I have learned along the way.
Why Europe acts in some crises but not others
It is often said that Europe only moves in a crisis. Jean Monnet wrote that Europe would be forged in crises, and would be the sum of the solutions adopted for them. The idea was that Europe has a kind of in-built inertia that only a crisis can overcome.
My experience of the past seven years is that this is only partly true. Europe responds decisively to some crises and hesitantly to others.
When events convince us that the world has changed, we act. During my term, I have watched Europe break one taboo after another.
Before the pandemic, few believed that the EU would ever borrow on a large scale in its own name. But once we accepted that no country could recover on its own, we created a recovery fund financed by common debt to the tune of €800 billion.
Europe was also said to be unable to take its own security seriously. Yet when Germany concluded that it would have to take on more of its own defence, it made the biggest change to its defence spending in generations. At the European level, we also agreed on Security Action for Europe (SAFE), which offers up to €150 billion in loans for joint defence procurement. And after decades of neutrality, Finland and Sweden joined NATO.
Nor did many expect Europe to act as a geopolitical power. Yet it is now Ukraine’s largest supporter. And when it became clear that Europe would have to bear more of the cost, the countries ready to act found a new way to borrow together on Ukraine’s behalf, even though not every country was ready to take part. Hence the coalition of the willing.
What made these steps possible? In each case, the cost of inaction was there for all to see, and it was plainly greater than the cost of acting. Once we were convinced of that, our institutions did not hold us back.
Our difficulties arise when a crisis moves slowly. The cost of inaction is then just as real, but it is far less visible. It builds up a little each year, and no single moment forces a decision. Meanwhile, the cost of acting is certain and has to be paid straight away.
Both the old challenges and the new ones are of this kind.
Take capital markets. We have all agreed for more than a decade that Europe needs a capital markets union. But building it means taking on vested interests now, for gains that arrive years later.
Each year without it, more of our savings are invested abroad and more of our growing firms look elsewhere for funding. Yet no single year’s loss is large enough to overcome the resistance to change.
We have seen this again in recent weeks. The Council has just agreed its position on strengthening the supervision of capital markets, which is welcome. But the position weakens the European supervisor’s ability to take effective decisions and includes too many carve-outs.
Our dependencies raise the same problem. Reducing them means paying for new capacity now, against a threat that may never materialise. One recent estimate suggests that raising Europe’s share of the world’s AI computing capacity from around 5% to 15% by 2030 would require investment of around €1.3 trillion.[1]
But as long as we can buy computing power from foreign providers and frontier AI models remain available to us, the case for paying that price is hard to make.
In both, the cost of inaction is real, whether it is a loss we are already suffering or a danger we may face tomorrow. But it rarely becomes visible enough to build the broad consensus for change that we found for the pandemic or for Ukraine.
This is the central problem of European policymaking. We can see the problem early, but we can act only once it has become impossible to ignore. And by then, almost by definition, it is too late. Lost industries are very hard to win back, and once a dependency has been used against us, our sovereignty is already exposed.
Think of the euro area debt crisis. The scale of Greece’s difficulties was clear long before Europe acted decisively to strengthen its institutions. We paid a much higher price than if we had acted earlier, including a six-quarter recession.
We often hear that policymakers in Europe do not understand the problems they face. I think they do. The difficulty is that they are asked to impose visible costs on their citizens today, for benefits that will only become apparent over time, before a majority is convinced that action is needed.
These are among the hardest decisions in public life, and I have a great deal of sympathy for those who have to take them.
At the ECB, we have had to take some of them too.
Acting early at the ECB
Economic sovereignty is not an objective in itself for us. Our primary objective is price stability, and the Treaty also gives us the tasks of issuing money and promoting the smooth operation of payment systems. But a changing world bears directly on those tasks, and during my term it has confronted us with slow-moving risks of our own.
We have faced decisions of this kind in three areas. In each, we had to choose whether to invest early in something whose value would only become clear later.
The first area was retail payments.
Since the euro was introduced, Europeans have had a single means of payment that works everywhere in the euro area: euro cash. But for card payments, we have relied on providers from outside Europe. International card schemes handle more than 60% of our card payments, and 14 of the 21 euro area countries have no domestic scheme at all.[2]
For a long time, this did not seem to matter, because cash was still the dominant means of payment. The international schemes worked well, and no one had ever cut Europe off.
The private sector tried more than once to build a European alternative, but each attempt ran into the same vicious circle: merchants will not adopt a scheme that few customers use, and customers will not use one that few merchants accept.
But cash is playing a smaller role as more of our spending moves online, where more than a third of our day-to-day spending now takes place.[3] And the geopolitical climate has changed. We have already seen judges of the International Criminal Court living in Europe, some of them European citizens, lose the use of their bank cards overnight.
So we concluded that Europe needed a digital equivalent of cash: the digital euro.
It will give Europeans a means of payment that runs on European infrastructure. And as legal tender, it will have to be accepted throughout the euro area wherever digital payments are possible, which will break the vicious circle in a way that private initiatives could not. Private payment providers will then have open rails on which to compete.
Because a project of this scale takes years to build, we had to start well before the need became pressing. If the legislation is adopted by the end of this year, we aim to be ready for a first issuance in 2029.
The second area was wholesale markets.
With blockchain technology, securities can now be tokenised, so that they are issued, traded and settled on a single platform. With the right framework, tokenisation offers a chance to build a genuine single market in digital assets, integrated from the start. For Europe, that is a huge opportunity.
But the window for seizing it is limited. The market for tokenised assets is still small, worth around €23 billion worldwide in March, but it was five times its size a year earlier.[4] As it grows, its standards and practices will take shape.
If they develop separately, the market could split into platforms that follow different rules and cannot settle with one another. And as our capital markets have taught us, once standards and practices have diverged, they are very hard to bring back together.
That is why, in September, we launched Pontes, which allows tokenised transactions to settle in central bank money on Eurosystem infrastructure, under European rules. Every platform now has access to a common settlement asset, so liquidity no longer has to be divided between them. Earlier this month, the European Stability Mechanism settled a €1 billion digitally native bond on Pontes.
Through Appia, we are working with market participants towards an integrated European market, including common standards. But infrastructure alone is not enough. Common rules will be needed too, and those lie with legislators.
The third area was the international role of the euro.
For most of its history, the ECB took a neutral view of the euro’s international role. Shortly before my term began, it moved to a more supportive line, and during my term we have acted on it. A stronger international role for the euro matters for our monetary policy, and it can support Europe’s growth and sovereignty in the world we now face.
Europe faces large investment needs, from defence to the technologies on which our autonomy depends, and a currency that investors around the world want to hold lowers the cost of financing them. In a world of more frequent shocks, the more of our trade is invoiced in euro, the less exposed we are to swings in exchange rates.
So, where it supports our own mandate, we have made the euro easier to use abroad.
We are linking TIPS, our instant payment system, with fast payment systems in other regions. We have also strengthened our international liquidity lines as a backstop. In February we made EUREP, our repo facility for central banks, permanent and open to central banks worldwide. More than 30 central banks have already expressed interest. And we are working to keep our swap lines fit for purpose in a more fragmented world. They will be more accessible, too.

Item 8.01 Other Events. 
As previously reported, under News Corporation's (the "Company's") stock repurchase program (the "Repurchase Program"), the Company is authorized to acquire from time to time up to $1 billion in the aggregate of the Company's outstanding shares of Class A common stock and Class B common stock. Under the rules of the Australian Securities Exchange (the "ASX"), the Company is required to provide to the ASX, on a daily basis, disclosure of transactions pursuant to the Repurchase Program, if any. The Company also discloses information concerning the Repurchase Program in the Company's quarterly and annual reports.
Attached as Exhibit 99.1 and Exhibit 99.2 are copies of the information provided to the ASX on the respective dates noted therein. Such information contains "forward-looking statements" within the meaning of the Private Securities Litigation Reform Act of 1995. These forward-looking statements include, but are not limited to, statements regarding the Company's intent to repurchase, from time to time, the Company's Class A common stock and Class B common stock. These statements are based on management's current expectations and beliefs and are subject to uncertainty and changes in circumstances. Actual results may vary materially from those expressed or implied by such statements due to, among other factors, changes in the market price of the Company's stock, general market conditions, applicable securities laws and alternative investment opportunities, as well as the risks, uncertainties and other factors described in the Company's filings with the Securities and Exchange Commission. The "forward-looking statements" included in such information are made only as of the date of this report. We do not have and do not undertake any obligation to publicly update any "forward-looking statements" to reflect subsequent events or circumstances, and we expressly disclaim any such obligation, except as required by law or regulation.

ITEM 1.01 ENTRY INTO A MATERIAL DEFINITIVE AGREEMENT. 
On November 19, 2026, Intuit Inc. (“Intuit”) entered into an Equity and Asset Purchase Agreement (the “Purchase Agreement”) with Bending Spoons US Inc., a Delaware corporation (“Purchaser”) and an indirect subsidiary of Bending Spoons S.p.A., an Italian joint stock company (società per azioni) (“Parent”), pursuant to which Intuit has agreed to sell its Mailchimp business (the “Business”) to Purchaser (the “Transaction”). The Transaction will be effected through the sale of all of the outstanding equity interests of The Rocket Science Group LLC, a Georgia limited liability company and wholly-owned subsidiary of Intuit, together with certain assets and liabilities of the Business held by Intuit and its other subsidiaries. 
Upon the terms and subject to the conditions set forth in the Purchase Agreement, Purchaser has agreed to pay an all-cash base purchase price of $3.68 billion, subject to customary adjustments for cash, indebtedness, net working capital and transaction expenses. 
Concurrently with the Purchase Agreement, Intuit entered into an Investment Agreement with Parent pursuant to which Intuit has agreed to invest approximately $368 million of the purchase price in Parent in exchange for 8,818,595 newly issued ordinary shares of Parent at the closing of the Transaction (the “Closing”). 
The consummation of the Transaction is subject to customary closing conditions, including (a) the expiration or termination of the waiting period under the Hart-Scott-Rodino Antitrust Improvements Act of 1976, as amended, and receipt of certain other specified regulatory approvals, (b) the absence of any law or order that prohibits the Transaction or imposes a Burdensome Condition (as defined in the Purchase Agreement), (c) the absence of a continuing material adverse effect with respect to the Business and (d) subject to certain materiality exceptions, the accuracy of each party’s representations and warranties and each party’s compliance with its covenants under the Purchase Agreement. The Transaction does not require the approval of Intuit’s shareholders and is not subject to a financing condition. Subject to the satisfaction or waiver of the conditions contained in the Purchase Agreement, the Transaction is expected to close in early calendar year 2027. 
The Purchase Agreement contains representations, warranties, and covenants of the parties customary for transactions of this type. Prior to the Closing, Intuit has agreed, subject to certain exceptions, to operate the Business in the ordinary course and not to solicit, negotiate or enter into alternative transactions relating to the Business. For two years following the Closing, Intuit has agreed not to engage in a competing business and each of Intuit and Purchaser has agreed to certain non-solicitation and non-disparagement provisions. Each party has agreed to indemnify the other party, subject to certain limitations, for breaches of its covenants, its fraud, and the liabilities it retains or assumes in the Transaction. 
The Purchase Agreement contains certain termination rights for Purchaser and Intuit, including: (a) by mutual written consent; (b) by either party if the Closing has not occurred on or before August 19, 2027, subject to a 3-month extension at the election of either party to obtain required regulatory approvals if all other closing conditions have been satisfied or waived (or are capable of being satisfied at such time); (c) by either party if a governmental authority has issued a final and non-appealable order that permanently prohibits the Transaction or imposes a Burdensome Condition (other than a Burdensome Condition that Purchaser, in its sole discretion, has determined to accept); and (d) by either party upon certain uncured breaches by the other party that would cause a closing condition to fail, in each case subject to the limitations set forth in the Purchase Agreement. 
In connection with the Closing, the parties will also enter into customary ancillary agreements, including an intellectual property license agreement and a transition services agreement. 
The foregoing description of the Purchase Agreement and the transactions contemplated thereby does not purport to be complete and is qualified in its entirety by reference to the Purchase Agreement, which is attached hereto as Exhibit 2.01 and incorporated herein by reference. The Purchase Agreement has been included to provide investors and securityholders with information regarding its terms and is not intended to provide any other factual information about Intuit, Purchaser or their respective subsidiaries and affiliates. The representations, warranties and covenants in the Purchase Agreement were made solely for the benefit of the parties thereto and are qualified by confidential disclosure schedules exchanged in connection with signing. Accordingly, investors and securityholders should not rely on the representations and warranties in the Purchase Agreement as characterizations of the actual state of facts or condition of Intuit, Purchaser, or their respective subsidiaries or affiliates. Moreover, information concerning the subject matter of the representations, warranties and covenants may change after the date of the Purchase Agreement, which subsequent information may or may not be fully reflected in public disclosures. 
Forward-Looking Statements 
This report contains forward-looking statements within the meaning of applicable securities laws. Forward-looking statements are often identified by the words “believe,” “expect,” “anticipate,” “plan,” “intend,” “foresee,” “should,” “would,” “could,” “may,” “estimate,” “outlook” and similar expressions, including the negative thereof. The absence of these words, however, does not mean that the statements are not forward-looking. 
Because these forward-looking statements involve risks and uncertainties, there are important factors that could cause our actual results to differ materially from the expectations expressed in the forward-looking statements. These factors include, without limitation: failure to obtain required regulatory approvals in a timely manner or at all; failure to satisfy any other closing conditions to the Transaction; the occurrence of any event, change or other circumstances that could give rise to the termination of the Purchase Agreement; risks related to separating the Business and providing transition services; disruption to management’s attention, our operations or our relationships with employees, customers and partners as a result of the Transaction; unanticipated costs or our inability to realize the anticipated benefits of the Transaction. More details about these and other risks that may impact our business are included in our Form 10-K for fiscal 2026 and in our other SEC filings. Item 5.02. Departure of Directors or Certain Officers; Election of Directors; Appointment of Certain Officers; Compensatory Arrangements of Certain Officers
On November 13, 2026, Mónica Gil notified NIKE, Inc. (the “Company”) of her decision to resign as a member of the Board of Directors of the Company (the “Board”) and the Compensation Committee of the Board, effective November 19, 2026. In connection with Ms. Gil’s resignation, the size of the Board will decrease to eleven directors, effective November 19, 2026. Ms. Gil was a director in good standing, and her decision to resign is not because of a disagreement with the Company or the Board on any matter relating to the Company’s operations, policies, or practices.
“We are appreciative of Mónica’s many contributions to the Board and to Nike over the last 4 years,” said Mark Parker, Executive Chairman of the Company.

Ladies and Gentlemen:
 | | 1. | Introductory. DUKE ENERGY Corporation, a Delaware
corporation (the “Corporation”), proposes, subject to the terms and conditions stated herein, to issue and sell $875,000,000
aggregate principal amount of 6.05% Senior Notes due 2036 (the “Notes”) to be issued pursuant to the provisions of
an Indenture, dated as of June 3, 2008, (the “Original Indenture”) as supplemented from time to time by supplemental
indentures, including the Thirty-eighth Supplemental Indenture, to be dated as of November 19, 2026 (the “Supplemental Indenture”
and, together with the Original Indenture, the “Indenture”), between the Corporation and The Bank of New York Mellon
Trust Company, N.A. (formerly known as The Bank of New York Trust Company, N.A.), as trustee (the “Trustee”). MUFG
Securities Americas Inc., PNC Capital Markets LLC, Santander US Capital Markets LLC, SMBC Nikko Securities America, Inc., U.S. Bancorp
Investments, Inc. and Wells Fargo Securities, LLC (the “Representatives”) are acting as representatives of the
several underwriters named in Schedule A hereto (together with the Representatives, the “Underwriters”). The Corporation
understands that the several Underwriters propose to offer the Notes for sale upon the terms and conditions contemplated by (i) this
Agreement and (ii) the Base Prospectus, the Preliminary Prospectus and the Permitted Free Writing Prospectus (each as defined below)
issued at or prior to the Applicable Time (as defined below) (the documents referred to in the foregoing subclause (ii) are referred
to herein as the “Pricing Disclosure Package”).
2.            Representations
and Warranties of the Corporation. The Corporation represents and warrants to, and agrees with, the several Underwriters that:
 | | (a) | A registration statement (No. 333-290475), as amended, including a prospectus, relating to the Notes
and certain other securities has been filed with the Securities and Exchange Commission (the “Commission”) under the
Securities Act of 1933, as amended (the “1933 Act”). Such registration statement and any post-effective amendment thereto,
each in the form heretofore delivered to you, became effective upon filing with the Commission pursuant to Rule 462 of the rules and
regulations of the Commission under the 1933 Act (the “1933 Act Regulations”), and no stop order suspending the effectiveness
of such registration statement has been issued and no proceeding for that purpose or pursuant to Section 8A of the 1933 Act has been
initiated or threatened by the Commission (if prepared, any preliminary prospectus supplement specifically relating to the Notes immediately
prior to the Applicable Time included in such registration statement or filed with the Commission pursuant to Rule 424(b) of
the 1933 Act Regulations being hereinafter called a “Preliminary Prospectus”); the term “Registration Statement”
means the registration statement as deemed revised pursuant to Rule 430B(f)(1) of the 1933 Act Regulations on the date of such
registration statement’s effectiveness for purposes of Section 11 of the 1933 Act, as such section applies to the Corporation
and the Underwriters for the Notes pursuant to Rule 430B(f)(2) of the 1933 Act Regulations (the “Effective Date”),
including all exhibits thereto and including the documents incorporated by reference in the prospectus contained in the Registration Statement
at the time such part of the Registration Statement became effective; the term “Base Prospectus” means the prospectus,
dated September 23, 2025, included in the Registration Statement; and the term “Prospectus” means the Base Prospectus
together with the prospectus supplement specifically relating to the Notes prepared in accordance with the provisions of Rule 430B
and promptly filed after execution and delivery of this Agreement pursuant to Rule 430B or Rule 424(b) of the 1933 Act
Regulations; any information included in such Prospectus that was omitted from the Registration Statement at the time it became effective
but that is deemed to be a part of and included in such registration statement pursuant to Rule 430B is referred to as “Rule 430B
Information;” and any reference herein to the Registration Statement, the Preliminary Prospectus or the Prospectus shall be
deemed to refer to and include the documents incorporated by reference therein, prior to the date hereof; any reference to any amendment
or supplement to any Preliminary Prospectus or Prospectus shall be deemed to refer to and include any documents filed after the date of
such Preliminary Prospectus or Prospectus, as the case may be, under the Securities Exchange Act of 1934, as amended (the “1934
Act”), and incorporated by reference in such Preliminary Prospectus or Prospectus, as the case may be; and any reference to
any amendment to the Registration Statement shall be deemed to refer to and include any annual report of the Corporation filed pursuant
to Section 13(a) or 15(d) of the 1934 Act after the effective date of the Registration Statement that is incorporated by
reference in the Registration Statement. For purposes of this Agreement, the term “Applicable Time” means 2:40 p.m. (New
York City time) on the date hereof.
2
 | | (b) | The Registration Statement, the Permitted Free Writing Prospectus specified on Schedule B hereto, the
Preliminary Prospectus and the Prospectus conform, and any amendments or supplements thereto will conform, in all material respects to
the requirements of the 1933 Act and the 1933 Act Regulations and the Registration Statement complied and will comply in all material
respects with the requirements of the Trust Indenture Act of 1939, as amended (the “1939 Act”), and the respective
rules and regulations thereunder; and (A) the Registration Statement, as of its original effective date and at each deemed effective
date with respect to the Underwriters pursuant to Rule 430B(f)(2) of the 1933 Act Regulations, and at the Closing Date (as defined
in Section 3), did not and will not contain any untrue statement of a material fact or omit to state any material fact required to
be stated therein or necessary to make the statements therein not misleading, and (B) (i) the Pricing Disclosure Package, as
of the Applicable Time, did not, (ii) the Prospectus and any amendment or supplement thereto, as of their dates, will not, and (iii) the
Prospectus as of the Closing Date will not, include any untrue statement of a material fact or omit to state any material fact necessary
to make the statements therein, in the light of the circumstances under which they were made, not misleading, except that the Corporation
makes no warranty or representation to the Underwriters with respect to any statements or omissions made in reliance upon and in conformity
with written information furnished to the Corporation by the Representatives on behalf of the Underwriters specifically for use in the
Registration Statement, the Permitted Free Writing Prospectus, the Preliminary Prospectus or the Prospectus.
 | | (c) | The Permitted Free Writing Prospectus specified on Schedule B hereto as of its issue date and at all subsequent
times through the completion of the public offer and sale of the Notes or until any earlier date that the Corporation notified or notifies
the Underwriters pursuant to Section 5(f) hereof did not, does not and will not include any information that conflicts with
the information (not superseded or modified as of the Effective Date) contained in the Registration Statement, the Preliminary Prospectus
or the Prospectus.
 | | (d) | At the earliest time the Corporation or another offering participant made a bona fide offer (within the
meaning of Rule 164(h)(2) of the 1933 Act Regulations) of the Notes, the Corporation was not an “ineligible issuer”
as defined in Rule 405 of the 1933 Act Regulations. The Corporation is, and was at the time of the initial filing of the Registration
Statement, eligible to use Form S-3 under the 1933 Act.
 | | (e) | The documents and interactive data in eXtensible Business Reporting Language (“XBRL”)
incorporated or deemed to be incorporated by reference in the Registration Statement, the Pricing Disclosure Package and the Prospectus,
at the time they were filed or hereafter are filed with the Commission, complied and will comply in all material respects with the requirements
of the 1934 Act and the rules and regulations of the Commission thereunder (the “1934 Act Regulations”), and,
when read together with the other information in the Prospectus, (a) at the time the Registration Statement became effective, (b) at
the Applicable Time and (c) on the Closing Date did not and will not contain an untrue statement of a material fact or omit to state
a material fact required to be stated therein or necessary to make the statements therein, in the light of the circumstances under which
they were made, not misleading.

by all necessary corporate action and the consummation of the transactions herein contemplated will not conflict with or result in a breach
or violation of any of the terms or provisions of, or constitute a default under, any indenture, mortgage, deed of trust, loan agreement

by which any of them or their respective property is bound or to which any of their properties or assets is subject that would have a
material adverse effect on the business, financial condition or results of operations of the Corporation and its subsidiaries, taken as
a whole, nor will such action result in any violation of the provisions of the amended and restated Certificate of Incorporation of the
Corporation (the “Certificate of Incorporation”), the amended and restated By-Laws of the Corporation (the “By-Laws”)
or any statute or any order, rule or regulation of any court or governmental agency or body having jurisdiction over the Corporation
or its Principal Subsidiaries or any of their respective properties that would have a material adverse effect on the business, financial
condition or results of operations of the Corporation and its subsidiaries, taken as a whole; and no consent, approval, authorization,
order, registration or qualification of or with any such court or governmental agency or body is required for the consummation by the
Corporation of the transactions contemplated by this Agreement, except for the approval of the North Carolina Utilities Commission which

and such consents, approvals, authorizations, registrations or qualifications as may be required under state securities or Blue Sky laws

Monetary Policy amid Frequent and Complex Shocks 
 Vice Chair Philip N. Jefferson 
At the International Monetary Fund and Central Bank of Brazil Conference “A Quarter Century of Inflation Targeting in Latin America: Progress, Challenges, and the Road Ahead,” Brasília, Brazil 
 Share 
 Watch Live 
Thank you, Nigel, for that kind introduction, and thank you to the Central Bank of Brazil and International Monetary Fund for hosting this important conference.1 It is an honor to be here with my fellow panelists. Today, I will briefly discuss issues that are critical for central bankers around the world—that is, how to assess and confront economic shocks. I discussed these issues in more depth in a speech earlier this year at Stanford University.2 
Shocks, by their nature, are difficult to predict and vary in length, but we are nonetheless very familiar with them. Just in the past few years, we have experienced a pandemic, a rapid rise in energy prices associated with geopolitical tensions, changes to trade policy, and a technological breakthrough. One way to classify shocks is to determine whether their initial effect is on the demand side or the supply side of the economy. Demand shocks affect spending by households, businesses, or the government without changing productive capacity. Supply shocks change productive capacity—what economists call "potential output"—by affecting the available supply of labor and capital or the productivity of those inputs. The nature and duration of these shocks influence the approach to monetary policymaking. 
As a monetary policymaker in the United States, I must consider whether and how shocks impact both sides of our dual mandate—maximum employment and stable prices. When a shock moves the output gap and inflation in the same direction, our objectives are aligned, and policy actions taken to address one also support the other.3 When a shock pushes them in opposite directions, there is a tradeoff. The recent rise in oil prices tied to the conflict in the Middle East is an example of the latter. An energy price shock can push up inflation while weighing on real incomes and demand. The appropriate response depends on the relative costs of missing each objective and the balance of risks. When the recent energy price shock occurred, inflation in the U.S. was already above our 2 percent target. If inflation expectations risk becoming unanchored, a stronger reaction to inflation is warranted. If price pressures are contained, it may be prudent to prioritize downside risks to employment. 
Shocks that affect both aggregate supply and aggregated demand but with differential timing are especially challenging for monetary policymakers. The rapid adoption of artificial intelligence (AI) represents such a shock. Business adoption of AI has risen considerably over the past two years.4 On the demand side, optimism about the technology has been boosting business investment in data centers, advanced computing equipment, and related products. On the supply side, AI is likely to automate some tasks and augment others, which could raise productivity and, in turn, the growth rate of potential output. Currently, the AI buildout is exerting upward pressure on demand and inflation. In the future, advancements in productivity could exert downward pressure on inflation while continuing to support growth. Labor market effects are relevant as well. AI could cause some job displacement, a meaningful challenge for affected households. Like many technological breakthroughs of the past, however, AI could lead to the creation of new jobs and new firms that we have not yet imagined. 
Shocks do not arrive in a vacuum. Energy, trade, and AI shocks are all unfolding at once. My colleagues at the Fed and my peers around the world must weigh them simultaneously. Our task is to remain attentive to our respective mandates and to keep the stance of our policies appropriately calibrated to achieve those stated goals. For the U.S. economy, my goal is to restore price stability while maintaining a solid labor market. That outcome will help the economy grow according to its full potential. 
Thank you, and I look forward to our discussion. 
1. The views expressed here are my own and are not necessarily those of my colleagues on the Federal Open Market Committee or the Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System. Return to text 
2. See Philip N. Jefferson, "Navigating Economic Shocks: A Monetary Policymaker's Perspective," speech delivered at the Stanford Institute for Economic Policy Research, Stanford University, Stanford, CA, July 16, 2026. Return to text 
3. The output gap is the difference between the economy's actual output, typically measured by GDP, and an estimate of its potential output. A positive gap signals excess demand, with employment above its maximum sustainable level and upward pressure on inflation; a negative gap signals excess supply, with the opposite effects. Return to text 
4. Recent technological advancements discussed in this speech are sometimes referred to as super intelligence or SI. Return to text

Cyber resilience guidance consultation and AI and quantum effective practices 
 UK’s financial regulators are proposing a new guidance to help financial services firms prepare for and recover from cyber incidents as threats grow. 
 Published on 
 19 November 2026 
News release
UK financial watchdogs clarify cyber expectations as attacks rise
UK’s financial regulators are proposing a new guidance to help financial services firms prepare for and recover from cyber incidents as threats grow.
The Bank of England’s (the Bank) latest Systemic Risk Survey cited cyber as one of the risks that would have the greatest impact on the UK financial system. October 2026 saw the second-highest monthly number of cyber incidents reported to the Financial Conduct Authority (FCA) in 5 years, 52% above the previous 18-month peak recorded in May 2025. 
In response, the Bank, FCA and Prudential Regulation Authority (PRA) are bringing together existing requirements and lessons from supervisory experience to give firms greater clarity about what is expected of them.
The proposed guidance aligns with recognised cyber frameworks, including the National Cyber Security Centre’s Cyber Assessment Framework. It sets out how firms should manage their cyber risk and resilience without imposing rigid rules, giving firms flexibility in how they meet the expectations in a fast evolving threat environment. 
It covers key areas, including how firms govern, identify, protect against, detect, respond to and recover from cyber risks and incidents. Firms need strong cyber controls to help keep them safe, support well-functioning markets and protect consumers.
Nikhil Rathi, Chief Executive of the FCA, said: 
'Technology moves fast, and so do cyber threats. The financial sector has a crucial role in tackling those threats, including through products like cyber insurance.
'Our response shouldn’t always be more rules. Firms have asked us for clarity about what good cyber resilience looks like. This guidance provides it, helping strengthen their resilience, protect clients and the services they rely on.'
Katharine Braddick, CEO of the PRA and Deputy Governor at the Bank of England, said:
'Cyber attacks are becoming more frequent, complex and dangerous. Regulators need confidence both that firms have strong cyber controls and that they can detect, contain and recover quickly from incidents. Today’s proposed guidance builds on latest understanding to help firms do that.' 
Dr Richard Horne, NCSC Chief Executive Officer, said: 
'We know cyber threats are becoming increasingly frequent and sophisticated, making it more important than ever that organisations can withstand and recover from cyber incidents. 
'The National Cyber Security Centre welcomes this proposed guidance, which will help firms better understand, assess, and strengthen their cyber resilience, in line with our Cyber Assessment Framework.'
Helping firms prepare for AI and quantum risks
Separately, the regulators are publishing additional ‘effective practices’, building on the cyber guidance to help firms practically prepare for specific cyber risks linked to rapid developments in AI and the potential emergence of quantum computing. 
The effective practices include firms tackling vulnerabilities to threat actors using AI, and encourage firms to consider the implications of quantum computing, which could undermine the public-key cryptography that underpins financial transactions. 
These materials reflect the regulators’ position and expertise that allows them to act on the newest risks in the sector, guiding firms through an uncertain and rapidly developing area.
Notes to editors
The consultation closes on 26 February 2027.
Firms, trade associations, technology providers and other interested stakeholders are encouraged to respond. Feedback will inform the final guidance next year.
The proposed guidance is appliable to firms in scope of the regulators' existing operational resilience requirements. 
The approach regulators have taken also reflects the FCA’s focus on smarter, proportionate regulation, providing greater clarity through guidance where new rules are not necessary. This gives firms flexibility in how they meet existing regulatory expectations as cyber risks continue to evolve.
The proposed guidance covers key foundational cyber risk and resilience areas including:
 - Embedding cyber risk and resilience in governance and risk management, with clear roles and accountabilities, appropriate Board and senior management oversight, defined risk appetite, and regular reporting and assurance.
 - Identifying and understanding critical IT infrastructure and cyber risk, maintaining up-to-date inventories and maps of critical assets, systems, data and dependencies, and assessing relevant threats, vulnerabilities and potential impacts.
 - Protecting critical IT infrastructure from cyber threats, applying proportionate controls including secure configuration, vulnerability and patch management, identity and access management, data protection, and controls over third parties and supply chains.
 - Detecting cyber events and incidents promptly, through effective monitoring and detection capabilities, defined alerting and escalation processes, and regular testing of firms' ability to identify potential attacks.
 - Responding to and recovering from cyber incidents effectively, with tested response and recovery plans, clear decision-making and communications arrangements, capabilities to contain attacks and restore services, and processes to identify and address lessons learned.
The additional material on AI and quantum computing is not open for formal consultation. However, the regulators are keen to understand from industry whether this type of support is useful and what they would like to see in future. See Effective practices: Cyber risk and resilience management relating to artificial intelligence (AI) and Effective practices: Cyber risk and resilience management relating to quantum computing.
A recent Bank of England and FCA survey, found 88% of respondents expect frontier AI cyber capabilities to have a moderate or high impact on their risk profile over the next 2 years.
In the same survey, 64% said vulnerability management and patching had seen the greatest increase in management attention due to awareness of frontier AI.

Minutes of the Market Participants Group meeting – 18 November 2026 
 The Market Participants Group (MPG) is a senior-level forum for financial market participants to share their views on relevant themes and narratives in financial markets with members of the Bank of England’s Monetary Policy Committee. 
 Published on 
 19 November 2026 
Time: 5pm – 6.30pm | Location: Bank of England
Published on 19 November 2026
Minutes 
Item 1 – Welcome
The Governor began the meeting by thanking attendees for joining and reminding participants of the purpose of these meetings. The Governor made clear that the MPC would be in listening mode, and that the meeting would be conducted in accordance with relevant competition and conduct laws, as per the terms of reference.
Item 2 – International developments
Market participants opened by discussing developments in major advanced economies outside the UK. The resilience of global growth and the strength of corporate sector balance sheets, particularly in the United States, were noted. Energy markets were also discussed, with market participants highlighting the inherent difficulty of forecasting energy prices amid continued geopolitical uncertainty.
The material support to global growth from AI-related capital expenditure was noted. Participants also discussed the increasing role of debt financing and the potential implications of a change in expectations around AI for risky asset markets, investment and consumption.
The discussion also covered potential financial market vulnerabilities arising from elevated hedge-fund leverage, sovereign debt pressures and cyber risks.
Item 3 – Domestic developments
Market participants discussed the outlook for the UK economy and the implications for monetary policy. Participants noted the resilience of UK growth this year despite the energy shock. This resilience was broadly seen to have strengthened the case for higher rates, with the November increase having been widely expected. Growth in global AI-related investment was noted as one factor supporting UK activity, although there was some discussion over the extent to which the resilience in domestic growth would persist. Participants also discussed the implications of AI-related growth for domestic inflationary pressure. 
Market participants noted the correlation between energy prices and market rates, and how this relationship had evolved over recent months. In discussing the implications of the energy shock, views differed on the relative importance of its demand and supply-side effects. The distinction between implied pricing in the market curve and modal expectations for policy was also noted by market participants.

Palo Alto Networks Reports Fiscal First Quarter 2027 Financial Results
SANTA CLARA, Calif., Nov. 18, 2026 — Palo Alto Networks® (NASDAQ: PANW), the global AI cybersecurity leader, announced today financial results for its fiscal first quarter ended October 31, 2026.
"We had a strong start to the year with a record Q1 and delivered one of our highest NGS ARR beats ever as our customers turn to us to protect them against an unprecedented threat environment," said Nikesh Arora, chairman and chief executive officer of Palo Alto Networks. "As AI reshapes the threat landscape, we must continually evolve to protect our customers and enable them to adopt AI securely. To that end, we are pleased to announce our intent to acquire Applied Compute, which will allow us to deliver secure open weight models to our customers and accelerate the adoption of enterprise AI."
"We delivered a very strong start to the year, in what is typically a seasonally slower Q1, fueled by acceleration across each of our segments," said Dipak Golechha, chief financial officer of Palo Alto Networks. "Given the current threat environment and demand we see ahead of us, we are materially raising our full year guidance."
First Quarter Fiscal 2027 Financial Highlights
•Total revenue for the fiscal first quarter 2027 grew 39% year over year to $3.44 billion.
•Next-Generation Security ARR for the fiscal first quarter 2027 grew 66% year over year to $9.73 billion.
•Remaining performance obligations grew 35% year over year to $21.0 billion.
•GAAP operating income for the fiscal first quarter 2027 was $96 million, compared with GAAP operating income of $309 million for the fiscal first quarter 2026. Non-GAAP operating income for the fiscal first quarter 2027 was $1.1 billion, compared with non-GAAP operating income of $746 million for the fiscal first quarter 2026. A reconciliation between GAAP and non-GAAP information is contained in the tables below.
•GAAP net income for the fiscal first quarter 2027 was $482 million, or $0.57 per diluted share, compared with GAAP net income of $334 million, or $0.47 per diluted share, for the fiscal first quarter 2026. Non-GAAP net income for the fiscal first quarter 2027 was $881 million, or $1.05 per diluted share, compared with non-GAAP net income of $662 million, or $0.93 per diluted share, for the fiscal first quarter 2026. A reconciliation between GAAP and non-GAAP information is contained in the tables below.
•Net cash provided by operating activities for the fiscal first quarter 2027 was $1.9 billion, compared with net cash provided by operating activities of $1.8 billion for the fiscal first quarter 2026. Adjusted free cash flow for fiscal first quarter 2027 was $1.9 billion, compared with adjusted free cash flow of $1.7 billion for the fiscal first quarter 2026. Fiscal first quarter 2027 adjusted free cash flow margin was 56.2%. A reconciliation between GAAP and non-GAAP information is contained in the tables below.
Today, Palo Alto Networks announced its intent to acquire Applied Compute, a leading platform for post-training and inference of open-weight AI models. More information can be found here (investors.paloaltonetworks.com/news-releases/news-release-details/palo-alto-networks-acquire-applied-compute-bringing-secure-open).
Financial Outlook
Palo Alto Networks provides guidance based on current market conditions and expectations.
For the fiscal second quarter 2027, we expect:
•Next-Generation Security ARR of $10.20 billion to $10.22 billion, representing year-over-year growth of 61%.
•Remaining performance obligations of $21.5 billion to $21.6 billion, representing year-over-year growth of 34% to 35%.
•Total revenue in the range of $3.530 billion to $3.550 billion, representing year-over-year growth of 36% to 37%.
•Diluted non-GAAP net income per share in the range of $1.01 to $1.03, using 837 million to 842 million shares outstanding.
For the fiscal year 2027, we expect:
•Next-Generation Security ARR of $11.475 billion to $11.525 billion, representing year-over-year growth of 26% to 27%.
•Remaining performance obligations of $25.3 billion to $25.5 billion, representing year-over-year growth of 19% to 20%.
•Total revenue in the range of $14.52 billion to $14.57 billion, representing year-over-year growth of 26% to 27%.
•Non-GAAP operating margin of 29.5%.
•Diluted non-GAAP net income per share in the range of $4.26 to $4.30, using 844 million to 847 million shares outstanding.
•Adjusted free cash flow margin to be 38.0%.
Guidance for non-GAAP financial measures excludes share-based compensation-related charges, including share-based payroll tax expense, acquisition-related costs, including change in fair value of contingent consideration liability, amortization expense of acquired intangible assets, litigation-related charges, change in fair value of convertible senior notes and capped calls, and income tax and other tax adjustments related to our long-term non-GAAP effective tax rate, along with certain non-recurring expenses and certain non-recurring cash flows. We have not reconciled non-GAAP operating margin guidance to GAAP operating margin, diluted non-GAAP net income per share guidance to GAAP net income per diluted share, or adjusted free cash flow margin guidance to GAAP net cash provided by operating activities because we do not provide guidance on GAAP operating margin, GAAP net income or net cash provided by operating activities and would not be able to present the various reconciling cash and non-cash items between GAAP and non-GAAP financial measures because certain items that impact these measures are uncertain or out of our control, or cannot be reasonably predicted, including share-based compensation expense, without unreasonable effort. The actual amounts of such reconciling items will have a significant impact on the company’s GAAP net income per diluted share, GAAP operating margin and GAAP net cash provided by operating activities.
Earnings Call Information
Palo Alto Networks will host a video webcast for analysts and investors to discuss the company’s fiscal first quarter 2027 results as well as the outlook for its fiscal second quarter and fiscal year 2027 today at 4:30 p.m. Eastern time/1:30 p.m. Pacific time. Open to the public, investors may access the webcast, supplemental financial information and earnings slides from the "Investors" section of the company’s website at investors.paloaltonetworks.com. A replay will be available three hours after the conclusion of the webcast and archived for one year.
Forward-Looking Statements
This press release contains forward-looking statements that involve risks, uncertainties and assumptions including statements regarding our financial and operating results and financial outlook for the fiscal second quarter 2027 and fiscal year 2027 and statements regarding the proposed acquisition of Applied Compute. There are a significant number of factors that could cause actual results to differ materially from forward-looking statements made or implied in this press release, including: the effect of the announcement of the proposed acquisition on the parties’ commercial relationships and workforce; the ability to satisfy the conditions to the closing of the acquisition; the ability to consummate the proposed acquisition on a timely basis or at all; significant and/or unanticipated difficulties, liabilities or expenditures relating to the proposed acquisition; risks related to diversion of management time and attention from ongoing business operations due to the proposed acquisition; our ability to effectively operate Applied Compute operations and business following the closing, integrate Applied Compute’s business and products with our products and services following the closing, and realize the anticipated benefits and synergies of the transaction in a timely manner or at all; unfavorable economic and market conditions and the uncertain geopolitical environment; our ability to effectively manage future growth and improve our systems, processes, and controls; our ability to maintain our revenue growth rate or profitability; variability and seasonality in our operating results; our ability to sell new and additional products, subscriptions, and support offerings to existing and new customers; the 
delayed recognition of revenue from subscription and support offerings; revenue volatility from consumption- or usage-based offerings and customer usage optimization behavior; potential decreases in the sales prices of our products, subscriptions, and support offerings; our reliance on channel partners; credit and liquidity risk exposure; challenges associated with sales to government entities; intense competition in our markets; risks associated with the evolving definition of the identity security market; customer trends toward vendor consolidation in cybersecurity; competition from cloud infrastructure providers offering native security capabilities; risks related to past and future acquisitions; our ability to predict, prepare for, and respond to rapidly evolving technological and market developments; the need to maintain a broad ecosystem of third-party technology integrations; risks related to the development, deployment, or use of AI, including AI agents as a new class of identity; the impact of network or data security incidents; defects, errors, or vulnerabilities in our products and subscriptions; reliance on customers to configure and use our products securely; the quality of our technical support services; our ability to meet service-level commitments; our reliance on data center facilities operated by third-party cloud service providers; intellectual property claims and our ability to protect proprietary rights; risks associated with open source software; our reliance on third-party technology licenses; dependence on manufacturing partners and limited sources of supply; our ability to attract, retain, and motivate key personnel; risks associated with international sales and operations, including export and import controls; fluctuations in foreign currency exchange rates; risks associated with operations and employees located in Israel; costs and risks related to compliance with privacy and data protection laws; potential tax liabilities; risks related to estimates, judgments, and critical accounting policies; our ability to maintain proper and effective internal control over financial reporting; risks related to corporate responsibility matters; dilution from issuance of additional common stock; risks related to our convertible senior notes, including our ability to settle conversions, repurchase, or repay such notes and the potential effect of capped call transactions.
Additional risks and uncertainties on these and other factors that could affect our financial results and cause actual results to differ materially from those described in the forward-looking statements we make in this press release are included under the captions "Risk Factors" and "Management's Discussion and Analysis of Financial Condition and Results of Operations" in our annual reports on Form 10-K and quarterly reports on Form 10-Q, which are available on our website at investors.paloaltonetworks.com and on the SEC's website at www.sec.gov. Additional information and risks and uncertainties will also be set forth in other documents that we file with or furnish to the SEC from time to time. INFORMATION TO BE INCLUDED IN THE REPORT 
ITEM 1.01 Entry into a Material Definitive Agreement 
On November 16, 2026, Consolidated Edison, Inc. (“Con Edison”) entered into a forward sale agreement (the “Forward Sale Agreement”) with Bank of America, N.A. (the “Forward Purchaser”) relating to 6,000,000 of Con Edison’s Common Shares ($0.10 par value) (the “Common Shares”). In connection with the execution of the Forward Sale Agreement and at our request, an affiliate of the Forward Purchaser is borrowing from third parties and selling Common Shares pursuant to the underwriting agreement relating to the Common Shares described in Item 8.01, below. 
Con Edison expects the Forward Sale Agreement to settle by December 31, 2027; however, the Forward Sale Agreement may be settled earlier in whole or in part at Con Edison’s option, subject to the satisfaction of certain conditions. In addition, the Forward Purchaser may accelerate the Forward Sale Agreement upon the occurrence of certain events. On a settlement date, if Con Edison decides to physically settle the Forward Sale Agreement, Con Edison will issue Common Shares to the Forward Purchaser under the Forward Sale Agreement at the then-applicable forward price. The forward price initially is equal to $119.81 per share. The Forward Sale Agreement provides that the forward price will be subject to adjustment on a daily basis based on a floating interest rate factor equal to the overnight bank funding rate less a spread, and will be subject to decrease on each of certain dates by amounts related to expected dividends on the Common Shares during the term of the Forward Sale Agreement. If the overnight bank funding rate is less than the spread on any day, the interest factor will result in a daily reduction of the forward price. 
The Forward Sale Agreement will be physically settled, unless Con Edison elects cash settlement or net share settlement under the Forward Sale Agreement (which it has the right to do, subject to certain conditions, other than in the limited circumstances described below and set forth in the Forward Sale Agreement). In the event Con Edison elects to cash settle or net share settle, the settlement amount will be generally related to (1)(a) the market value of the Common Shares during the unwind period under the Forward Sale Agreement minus (b) the applicable adjusted forward price; multiplied by (2) the number of Common Shares underlying the Forward Sale Agreement subject to such cash settlement or net share settlement. If this settlement amount is a negative number, the Forward Purchaser will pay Con Edison the absolute value of that amount or deliver to Con Edison a number of Common Shares having a value equal to the absolute value of such amount. If this settlement amount is a positive number, Con Edison will pay the Forward Purchaser that amount or deliver to the Forward Purchaser a number of Common Shares having a value equal to such amount. 
The Forward Purchaser will have the right to accelerate the Forward Sale Agreement (with respect to all or any portion of the transaction under the Forward Sale Agreement that the Forward Purchaser determines is affected by such event) and require Con Edison to settle on a date specified by the Forward Purchaser if: (1) the Forward Purchaser determines it is unable, after using commercially reasonable efforts, to borrow (or maintain a borrowing of) a number of Common Shares equal to the number of Common Shares underlying the Forward Sale Agreement at a rate that is equal to or less than the borrow cost specified in the Forward Sale Agreement; (2) the Forward Purchaser determines that it has an excess Section 13 ownership position or an excess regulatory ownership position (as such terms are defined in the Forward Sale Agreement) with respect to certain ownership restrictions and related filing requirements under the federal securities laws, the New York business corporation law or certain other laws and regulations, as applicable; (3) Con Edison declares or pays certain dividends or distributions on the Common Shares with a cash value in excess of a specified amount, an ex-dividend date that occurs earlier than a specified date or certain non-cash dividends; (4) there occurs the announcement of any event or transaction that, if consummated, would result in a merger event, tender offer, nationalization, delisting or change in law (in each case, as determined pursuant to the terms of the Forward Sale Agreement); (5) the scheduled maturity occurs during an unwind period related to a cash settlement or net share settlement for all or any portion of the transaction under the forward sale agreement; or (6) certain other events of default, termination events or other specified events occur, including, among other things, any material misrepresentation made by Con Edison in connection with entering into the Forward Sale Agreement or a market disruption event during a specified period that lasts for at least eight consecutive scheduled trading days (in each case, as determined pursuant to the terms of the Forward Sale Agreement). The Forward Purchaser’s decision to exercise its right to accelerate the settlement of the Forward Sale Agreement will be made irrespective of Con Edison’s interests, including Con Edison’s need for capital. In such cases, Con Edison could be required to issue and deliver Common Shares under the physical settlement provisions, which would result in dilution to Con Edison’s earnings per share and return on equity. In addition, upon certain 
events of bankruptcy or insolvency relating to Con Edison, the Forward Sale Agreement will terminate. Following any such termination, Con Edison may not issue any Common Shares and it would not receive any proceeds pursuant to the Forward Sale Agreement. 
The description of the Forward Sale Agreement set forth above does not purport to be complete and is qualified in its entirety by reference to the terms and conditions of the Forward Sale Agreement, which is filed as an exhibit hereto. 
ITEM 8.01. Other Events 
On November 16, 2026, Con Edison entered into an underwriting agreement with BofA Securities, Inc., acting in its capacity as the underwriter, and BofA Securities, Inc., acting in its capacity as the forward seller, and the Forward Purchaser for the sale of 6,000,000 Common Shares. The Common Shares were registered under the Securities Act of 1933 pursuant to a Registration Statement on Form S-3 (No. 333-286304, effective April 1, 2025). 
The information in this report includes forward-looking statements. The forward-looking statements reflect information available and assumptions at the time the statements are made, and accordingly speak only as of that time. Actual results or developments might differ materially from those included in the forward-looking statements because of various factors including, but not limited to, those identified in reports Con Edison has filed with the Securities and Exchange Commission.

RAHWAY, N.J., Nov. 18, 2026 – Merck (NYSE: MRK), known as MSD outside the United States and Canada, today announced that Thomas H. Glocer intends to retire from the Merck Board of Directors at the Company’s Annual Meeting of Shareholders in May 2027. The independent members of the Board have appointed Douglas M. Baker, Jr., as independent lead director, effective Jan. 1, 2027, succeeding Mr. Glocer in the role.
Mr. Baker has served on the Merck Board of Directors since 2022. He has wide-ranging expertise in corporate governance and organizational management, including a deep understanding of global marketing, sales and operations of public companies. Previously, Mr. Baker was chairman and chief executive officer of Ecolab Inc., a provider of water and hygiene services and technologies for the food, hospitality, industrial and energy markets. He is also a trustee of Mayo Clinic. 
“Merck has counted on Tom’s expertise and counsel as a trusted voice in our boardroom for many years, and I have relied on him as a valued collaborator. His contributions to our Company have been invaluable, and on behalf of everyone at Merck, I thank him for his dedicated service,” said Rob Davis, chairman and chief executive officer, Merck. “As we look ahead, Doug is a thoughtful, experienced and accomplished leader who will undoubtedly serve the Board well in this expanded role. I look forward to our continued work together as we deliver value to our stakeholders.”
 About Merck
At Merck, known as MSD outside of the United States and Canada, we are unified around our purpose: We use the power of leading-edge science to save and improve lives around the world. For more than 130 years, we have brought hope to humanity through the development of important medicines and vaccines. We aspire to be the premier research-intensive biopharmaceutical company in the world — and today, we are at the forefront of research to deliver innovative health solutions that advance the prevention and treatment of diseases in people and animals. We foster a diverse global workforce and operate responsibly every day to enable a safe, sustainable and healthy future for all people and communities. For more information, visit www.merck.com and connect with us on 
X (formerly Twitter), Facebook, Instagram, YouTube and LinkedIn.

Air Products to Nominate Carol Williams for Election to Board of Directors 
LEHIGH VALLEY, PA (November 18, 2026) – Air Products (NYSE: APD) today announced that it will nominate Carol Williams as an independent director
candidate for election to its Board of Directors at the Company’s 2027 Annual Meeting of Shareholders. 
Williams brings significant industry and
operational experience, including senior leadership of manufacturing, engineering, supply chain, and environmental, health and safety functions at The Dow Chemical Company. 
“We are delighted to nominate Carol, a proven leader who would be a strong addition to the Board as it oversees Air Products’ strategy and
continued focus on safe, reliable execution to deliver long-term value for shareholders,” said Wayne T. Smith, Chairman of the Board. 
Williams spent 34 years at Dow in roles that included Executive Vice President of Manufacturing and Engineering, Supply Chain and Environmental, Health and
Safety Operations; President of Chemicals and Energy; and Senior Vice President of Basic Chemicals. She retired at the end of 2014 as Special Advisor to the Chief Executive Officer. Williams serves on the boards of Olin Corporation, where she chairs
the Nominating and Governance Committee, and O-I Glass, Inc. She holds a bachelor’s degree in chemical engineering from Carnegie Mellon University. 
The Company also announced that Jessica Trocchi Graziano and Bhavesh (“Bob”) Patel will not stand for
re-election at the 2027 Annual Meeting and will retire from the Board when their terms conclude. 
“We are
grateful to Jessica and Bob for their service and contributions to Air Products,” said Smith. “Both provided important insight and counsel during a period of significant change for the Company, and we thank them for their dedication and
wish them well in their future endeavors.” 
About Air Products 
Air Products (NYSE: APD) is a world-leading industrial gases company in operation for more than 85 years. Serving energy, environmental, and emerging
markets, the Company is generating a cleaner future by providing essential industrial gases, related equipment, and applications expertise that help customers improve productivity, efficiency, and sustainability across a wide range of industries,
including energy, chemicals, electronics, metals, manufacturing, food, medical, and space. 
Air Products is focused on profitably growing its core
industrial gases business, accelerating growth in areas of competitive strength, and extending its reach through disciplined opportunities that create long-term value. As the leading global supplier of hydrogen, Air Products develops, engineers,
builds, owns and operates some of the world’s largest hydrogen projects and has extensive capabilities in air separation technology, engineering, and plant operations. Through its sale of equipment businesses, the Company also provides
specialized products such as turbomachinery, membrane systems, and cryogenic containers globally. 
Air Products had fiscal 2026 sales of $13.0 billion from operations in approximately 50 countries. For
more information, visit www.airproducts.com or follow us on LinkedIn, X, Facebook, or Instagram.

automatic shelf registration statement (the “Registration Statement”) on Form S-3 (File No. 333-299594 and
333-299594-01) and a preliminary prospectus supplement and prospectus supplement related to the offering of the Notes, each as previously

2026, entered into by and among the Company, Standard & Poor’s Financial Services LLC (the “Guarantor”) and
each of BofA Securities, Inc. and Goldman Sachs & Co. LLC, as representatives of the several underwriters named therein.
The Notes are governed by an indenture dated as
of May 26, 2015 (the “Base Indenture”), among the Company, the Guarantor and U.S. Bank Trust Company, National Association,
successor in interest to U.S. Bank National Association, as trustee (the “Trustee”), as supplemented by the eleventh supplemental
indenture dated as of November 18, 2026, among the Company, the Guarantor and the Trustee (the “Eleventh Supplemental Indenture,”
and together with the Base Indenture, the “Indenture”). Each series of the Notes is fully and unconditionally guaranteed by
the Guarantor on a senior unsecured basis (the “Guarantees” and, together with the Notes, the “Securities”).
The Company intends to use the net proceeds from
the Offering for general corporate purposes, which may include, without limitation, funding of possible acquisitions, repayment, redemption
or refinancing of indebtedness, capital expenditures, working capital, satisfaction of other obligations or repurchase of the Company’s
outstanding common stock. The Company may temporarily invest the net proceeds of this offering in short-term, liquid investments until
they are used for their stated purpose.
The terms of the Securities are governed by the
Indenture, which contains covenants that, among other things, limit the Company’s ability to (i) create, assume, incur or guarantee
any indebtedness for money borrowed secured by a lien on any of its properties or assets, without securing the Securities equally and
ratably with (or prior to) such secured indebtedness and (ii) consolidate with or merge into any other person or convey or transfer
its properties and assets substantially as an entirety to any person. The Company has the right to redeem the Securities at any time on
the terms provided in the Indenture. Upon the occurrence of a Change of Control Triggering Event, as defined in the Indenture, unless
the Company has exercised its right to redeem all of the Securities, each holder will have the right to require the Company to repurchase
its Securities at a purchase price equal to 101% of the aggregate principal amount thereof plus accrued and unpaid interest. The Indenture
also contains customary events of default. Indebtedness under the Securities may be accelerated in certain circumstances upon an event

Entry into a Material Definitive Agreement. 
Issuance of 5.850% Senior Notes due 2029 
On November 18, 2026, LPL Holdings, Inc. (the “Company”), a wholly-owned subsidiary of LPL Financial Holdings Inc. (the “Guarantor”), completed the issuance and sale of $750,000,000 aggregate principal amount of 5.850% Senior Notes due 2029 (the “Senior Notes”). The Senior Notes were issued pursuant to an Indenture, dated November 17, 2023, among the Company, the Guarantor and U.S. Bank Trust Company, National Association, as trustee (the “Base Indenture”), as supplemented by the Ninth Supplemental Indenture, dated November 18, 2026 (the “Ninth Supplemental Indenture,” and, together with the Base Indenture, the “Indenture”). The Indenture contains customary covenants and events of default. 
The Senior Notes are senior unsecured obligations of the Company and are fully and unconditionally guaranteed on a senior unsecured basis by the Guarantor. 
The sale of the Senior Notes has been registered with the Securities and Exchange Commission on the Company’s and the Guarantor’s shelf registration statement on Form S-3 (Registration Nos. 333-300064 and 333-300064-01) (the “Registration Statement”). 
The Company intends to use the net proceeds from the Senior Notes offering to repay outstanding borrowings under its revolving credit facility and for general corporate purposes. 
The Senior Notes will mature on November 16, 2029, and will bear interest at the rate of 5.850% per year, with interest payable semi-annually on May 16 and November 16 of each year, commencing on May 16, 2027. The Company may redeem all or part of the Senior Notes at any time and from time to time prior to October 16, 2029 (the “Par Call Date”) at a redemption price equal to the greater of: (1)(a) the sum of the present values of the remaining scheduled payments of principal and interest thereon discounted to the redemption date (assuming the Senior Notes matured on the Par Call Date) on a semi-annual basis (assuming a 360-day year consisting of twelve 30-day months) at the Treasury Rate (as defined in the Ninth Supplemental Indenture) plus 20 basis points less (b) interest accrued to, but excluding, the redemption date, and (2) 100% of the principal amount of the Senior Notes to be redeemed, plus, in either case, accrued and unpaid interest thereon to, but excluding, the redemption date. On or after the Par Call Date, the Company may redeem the Senior Notes, in whole or in part, at any time and from time to time, at a redemption price equal to 100% of the principal amount of the Senior Notes being redeemed plus accrued and unpaid interest thereon to, but excluding, the redemption date.
